svg.title: A production spanning tree baseline in five layers, beside the three MST details that must match character for character
svg.desc: Five stacked bars give a baseline: global defaults for mode, loop guard and BPDU guard; explicit root primary and secondary assignments per VLAN group; uplink settings for loop guard, UDLD and explicit cost; edge settings pairing PortFast with BPDU guard and storm control; and the verification commands with topology change counters. A box on the right lists the three MST details that must match exactly, name, revision and instance mapping, notes that a mismatch silently falls back to the common instance with no error logged, and gives the daily digest comparison as the only practical check.
svg.text: A spanning tree baseline is five layers of defaults, not three hundred lines of per-port intent
Anything configured port by port will be missing on the port that matters
GLOBAL
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree loopguard default
the mode sets the floor of what is possible
defaults protect the ports nobody remembered
ROOT
spanning-tree vlan 10,30 root primary
spanning-tree vlan 20,40 root secondary
split VLANs between the two switches,
so both uplinks carry traffic
UPLINK
guard loop, udld aggressive, explicit cost
fiber ports only: this is where a one-way link forms a loop STP cannot see
EDGE
switchport portfast + bpduguard, storm-control
always as a pair, always in the access template, never by hand
PROOF
show spanning-tree root / summary / detail
topology change counters per port, alarmed on rate, not on absolute value
MST: THREE DETAILS THAT MUST MATCH
1. region name — character for character,
including a trailing space nobody sees.
2. revision number — a single digit off
splits the region in two.
3. instance-to-VLAN mapping — differ, and
the load sharing you designed disappears.
A split region logs nothing. Every switch simply
falls back to the common instance and keeps going.
THE ONLY PRACTICAL CHECK
show spanning-tree mst configuration digest
Compare the digest daily, and before and after
every change. It is one line of evidence that the
region is still one region, readable in a script.
If the digest is not identical, treat the region as broken.
The baseline has three parts and only one of them is configuration: a template that carries the intent, a snapshot taken before each change, and an alarm on the counters.
MST consistency is an implicit contract — nothing enforces it, nothing reports it, and every switch looks locally correct while the design has quietly stopped working.
That is why the digest belongs in the daily report rather than in the runbook: it is the only check that fails before the users do.
